subject_name: Personal Savings Allowance and Starting Rate
intro: How much savings interest can be earned tax-free through the Personal Allowance, the starting rate for savings and the Personal Savings Allowance, and how the tax is collected.
explanation:
## Interest can be covered by three separate allowances

Interest on savings held outside an ISA can be taxable, but up to three allowances may cover some or all of it. The first is the Personal Allowance: whatever part of it is not used up by wages, a pension or other income is applied to savings interest by HMRC. Next come the starting rate for savings and the Personal Savings Allowance, which are separate allowances. A person may qualify for both of those at once, and either can sit alongside whatever Personal Allowance is left. Interest inside an ISA is not taxed at all.

## The starting rate for savings shrinks as other income rises

The starting rate for savings is up to {fact:starting_rate_savings_band} of tax-free interest for people with low other income. It is available only when other taxable income, which leaves out savings interest and dividends, is below {fact:starting_rate_income_limit}. Every £1 of other income above the Personal Allowance reduces it by £1, so it falls to nothing at that limit.

## The Personal Savings Allowance depends on the tax band

The allowance is {fact:psa_basic_rate} for basic rate taxpayers, {fact:psa_higher_rate} for higher rate taxpayers and {fact:psa_additional_rate} for additional rate taxpayers, who therefore pay tax on all their interest outside tax-free accounts. The band is worked out by adding the interest to other income, so interest itself can push someone into a higher band and a lower allowance. Interest beyond that allowance is charged at the taxpayer's normal Income Tax rate.

Interest on a joint account is split equally between the holders, unless HMRC is told it should be divided differently, and each holder's share counts towards their own allowance.

## The tax is usually collected through a tax code

After the tax year ends, banks and building societies tell HMRC how much interest they paid. A person who sends a Self Assessment return reports it there. Someone who is employed or has a pension and owes tax gets a tax calculation, usually between June and the end of November, and HMRC normally collects the tax through their tax code, which can also include an estimate for the current year. Where a tax code cannot be changed, a Simple Assessment letter is sent instead, and anyone who owes tax but has had no letter by the end of November has to contact HMRC. Very large amounts of interest have to be reported on a Self Assessment return, and HMRC sends a notice to file one when a bank reports them.

## Savings tax rates are due to rise from April 2027

From 6 April 2027 the rates of Income Tax on savings income are due to become {fact:savings_basic_rate_2027} at the basic rate, {fact:savings_higher_rate_2027} at the higher rate and {fact:savings_additional_rate_2027} at the additional rate. The Personal Savings Allowance and the starting rate for savings are not changing.
